business_patterns.top_pattern: CA HMO acute hospital spend is highly concentrated at UCI Medical Center
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CA HMO acute hospital inpatient spend
key_driver_codes: Cesarean Section without Sterilization with MCC
Intracranial Hemorrhage or Cerebral Infarction with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA HMO acute hospital costs increased by about $5.6M and the increase was overwhelmingly concentrated at UCI Medical Center. The signal reflects both more inpatient claims and higher paid amounts per admission, with smaller contributions from C-section, stroke, GI obstruction, and bronchitis/asthma episodes. This looks like a concentrated provider and hospital-cost issue rather than a broad statewide inpatient trend.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A single provider concentration of this size can materially change trend and is actionable through UM and contracting levers.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Launch a joint UM and network review of UCI Medical Center HMO inpatient utilization, admission patterns, level-of-care management, and contract payment performance.
evidence_summary: CA HMO acute hospital spend increased about $5.6M.
UCI Medical Center drove about $5.3M, or 95%, of the increase.
UCI claim volume increased by 257 and paid per admit increased by about $19K.
Smaller acute inpatient increases also appeared in C-section and stroke cases.

business_patterns.top_pattern: MO IP Med/Surg has rare high-cost stroke and hemorrhage cases
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: MO IP Med/Surg high-acuity neurologic admissions
key_driver_codes: Intracranial Hemorrhage or Cerebral Infarction with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: MO IP Med/Surg costs rose because of a small number of new high-cost neurologic admissions, centered on stroke and hemorrhage diagnoses. The increase is concentrated in severe cases rather than broad inpatient growth. This is a rare-case clinical severity pattern that needs case-level confirmation before any broad policy response.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Rare neurologic admissions can create sharp spend spikes and often require targeted case management rather than broad utilization actions.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Send these MO neurologic admissions for case-level clinical and coding review, and confirm catastrophic case management and discharge planning for the affected members.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The increase is driven by a small number of rare, low-baseline high-cost cases, so severity and coding should be confirmed before broader intervention.
evidence_summary: MO IP Med/Surg rare cases added about $0.6M.
Diagnoses I63319 and I63311 together added about $316K across 13 claims.
One I63542 case added about $104K by itself.
Paid per admit was materially higher across these severe neurologic cases.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA IP Med/Surg is seeing isolated catastrophic inpatient cases
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CA IP Med/Surg rare high-cost admissions
key_driver_codes: Pathological Fractures and Musculoskeletal and Connective Tissue Malignancy with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA IP Med/Surg costs increased because of a handful of very high-cost admissions, including a large UCI Medical Center malignancy-related case and smaller bowel, GI, and respiratory spikes. The pattern is concentrated in rare inpatient events rather than a broad inpatient case increase. These cases warrant targeted clinical review and severity confirmation.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: A few catastrophic inpatient cases can distort trend and require different actions than normal utilization growth.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Perform case-level clinical review on the CA high-cost IP Med/Surg admissions, starting with the UCI malignancy-related case and the bowel surgery outliers, to confirm severity and appropriate care pathways.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern is driven by low-volume, high-severity admissions with large per-case impact, so case classification and severity should be validated.
evidence_summary: CA IP Med/Surg rare cases added about $0.6M.
One UCI Medical Center case in a malignancy-related DRG added about $268K.
Bowel surgery-related diagnoses Z433 and K5732 added about $182K combined.
Additional GI obstruction and respiratory cases created smaller low-volume spikes.

business_patterns.top_pattern: MO PPO stroke-related spend is expanding into post-acute SNF care
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: MO PPO acute and SNF care for severe stroke-related episodes
key_driver_codes: Intracranial Hemorrhage or Cerebral Infarction with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: MO PPO spend is clustering around severe stroke-related episodes, with the larger increase occurring in free-standing SNF and a smaller added unit-cost increase in acute hospital care. The pattern points to care-continuum and post-acute economics, not just an isolated inpatient event. The main business levers are discharge routing, SNF utilization, and post-acute reimbursement.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Post-acute stroke costs can persist and compound if SNF placement and payment terms are not actively managed.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Review MO PPO discharge-to-SNF patterns for stroke cases and evaluate free-standing SNF reimbursement, length of stay, and network steerage opportunities.
evidence_summary: MO PPO free-standing SNF spend increased about $316K for stroke-related care.
SNF claim volume increased by 13 and paid per admit increased by about $24K.
MO PPO acute hospital stroke stays added another $67K with no claim growth.
The combined pattern suggests cost pressure across the acute-to-post-acute pathway.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA maternity costs are concentrated in severe C-section cases
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CA inpatient maternity and acute hospital C-section episodes
key_driver_codes: Cesarean Section without Sterilization with MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA maternity spend is being driven by a small set of severe C-section admissions, and a separate PPO acute hospital signal shows added unit-cost pressure on the same DRG. This is a focused high-acuity maternity pattern rather than broad OB volume growth. The right response is targeted review of severe maternal cases and related reimbursement performance.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: High-acuity maternity episodes are expensive and require different interventions than routine delivery volume management.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Have clinical and reimbursement teams jointly review severe CA C-section cases for maternal risk severity, case management opportunities, and payment performance on the C-section MCC DRG.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern is driven by a few rare high-cost maternity cases, so severity and episode classification should be confirmed before broader action.
evidence_summary: Severe CA C-section cases added about $205K across 3 rare maternity admissions.
Diagnoses O1404, O114, and O42113 each contributed about $62K to $74K.
A separate CA PPO acute hospital C-section unit-cost signal added about $63K despite one fewer claim.
The combined pattern is focused on severe maternity episodes, not general delivery growth.

business_patterns.top_pattern: NY EPO acute hospital spend shows both pricing and low-volume inpatient pressure
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: NY EPO acute hospital inpatient spend
key_driver_codes: Intracranial Hemorrhage or Cerebral Infarction with MCC
Major Small and Large Bowel Procedures without CC/MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: NY EPO acute hospital costs rose across a small set of inpatient episodes, with both additional cases and higher paid amounts per admission contributing. Bowel surgery and bronchitis/asthma added low-volume mixed pressure, while stroke-related admissions were purely price-led. This looks like a small but concentrated hospital pricing and utilization pocket.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Even a small EPO inpatient block can generate avoidable trend if price variance is not separated from true case growth.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Audit NY EPO inpatient payment variance for these DRGs and confirm whether contract terms, outlier reimbursement, or isolated case mix drove the per-admission increase.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern is low-volume and concentrated, so pricing and case classification should be confirmed before broader reimbursement action.
evidence_summary: NY EPO acute hospital spend increased about $159K.
Bowel surgery and bronchitis/asthma cases added about $90K across 2 claims.
Stroke-related admissions added about $69K with no claim growth, making part of the increase unit-cost-led.
All components are concentrated in a small inpatient book.

business_patterns.top_pattern: CA PPO acute hospital trend is mainly a utilization issue in bowel and respiratory admissions
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: CA PPO acute hospital inpatient spend
key_driver_codes: Major Small and Large Bowel Procedures without CC/MCC
business_patterns.pattern_details: CA PPO acute hospital spend increased primarily because of more inpatient cases, especially bowel surgery, GI obstruction, and bronchitis/asthma admissions. Per-admission cost pressure is present in part of the pattern, but the main near-term lever is utilization. This looks more like targeted admission growth than broad reimbursement deterioration.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: When utilization is the main driver, UM and care-pathway actions are usually more effective than broad pricing interventions.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Target CA PPO inpatient admission management for bowel and respiratory episodes and confirm whether the added admissions were clinically necessary and appropriately routed.
evidence_summary: CA PPO acute hospital spend increased about $170K.
Major bowel procedures added about $108K on 3 more claims while per-admission cost was slightly down.
GI obstruction and bronchitis/asthma added about $62K across 5 more claims.
The combined signal is more volume-led than broad price-led.

business_patterns.top_pattern: Prime Surgical Center growth is mixed with Not Mapped outpatient claims and needs validation first
business_patterns.what_is_impacting: Outpatient surgery and other Not Mapped outpatient claims across CA, NH, NV, NY, and CO

providers: PRIME SURGICAL CENTER OF NEWPORT BEACH

key_driver_codes: PRIME SURGICAL CENTER OF NEWPORT BEACH
business_patterns.pattern_details: Outpatient provider mix and classification need to be validated before business action. Prime Surgical Center of Newport Beach shows real PPO ASC growth in CA and in NH and NV, but CA outpatient surgery claims tied to the same provider are also appearing in Not Mapped clinical categories, and smaller Not Mapped buckets are present for lab and behavioral providers in CA, NY, and CO. This is a gating data-quality and provider-setup issue because network, authorization, and reimbursement actions could be misdirected if the claims are not classified correctly.
business_patterns.why_it_matters: Misclassified outpatient claims can distort provider mix, facility comparisons, and authorization targeting.
business_patterns.recommended_next_step: Run a focused data-quality and provider setup audit on Prime Surgical Center and the remaining Not Mapped outpatient claims to confirm facility type, place of service, benefit and authorization rules, and clinical classification before taking network or UM action.
business_patterns.validation_reason: The pattern includes repeated Not Mapped facility and clinical categories plus concentrated outpatient growth at a single provider, so claim classification and provider setup must be confirmed first.
evidence_summary: CA OP Surg claims at Prime Surgical Center in Not Mapped categories added about $232K across 5 one-off cases.
Prime Surgical Center also drove PPO ASC growth of about $137K in CA and another $114K across NH and NV.
Additional Not Mapped outpatient claims across LabCorp and Heritage in CA, NY, and CO added about $22K.
The mix of provider concentration and Not Mapped categories makes this a validation gate before policy or contracting action.

executive_summary.headline: Cost growth is led by a very large CA HMO hospital concentration at UCI Medical Center, followed by rare high-cost inpatient cases in CA and MO and a smaller but important outpatient mapping and provider-setup issue.
executive_summary.primary_business_message: The biggest business story is concentrated inpatient spend, not broad-based trend, with UCI Medical Center driving most of the CA HMO increase and severe stroke, Med/Surg, and maternity cases creating distinct high-cost pockets. A second theme is targeted operational pressure in MO SNF, NY EPO acute hospital, and CA PPO acute hospital books. Outpatient provider mix actions should wait until Prime Surgical Center and other Not Mapped claims are validated.
recommended_focus_order: CA HMO acute hospital concentration at UCI Medical Center
Rare high-cost IP Med/Surg and maternity cases in CA and MO
MO PPO stroke-related post-acute SNF pathway and NY EPO acute hospital pricing pocket
Prime Surgical Center and other Not Mapped outpatient claims validation
